documents: Leontarakis, Orfanos & Apostolopoulos 2023, Near Surface Geophysics 21:39-64 (published paper, PDF)

entry.evidence: a reliable 3D subsurface imaging in a complex and noisy near-surface environment becomes difficult when using the fully automated processing techniques

sequences.source_document: Leontarakis et al. 2023, Near Surface Geophysics 21:39-64

steps.action: Frame the problem: MASW roll-along resolves sharp lateral variations poorly, and fully automated surface-wave tomography picking is unreliable in noisy, complex near-surface settings, so a robust 3D approach for dense active networks is needed.
steps.quote: a complicated and noisy environment, such as the near-surface one, makes difficult the reliable 3D subsurface imaging

steps.action: Define the cross-correlogram (CC) of every receiver pair per shot and its geometric parameters, state the uniform-radial-wavefront assumption, compute all CCs, scrub them by coherency, offset and angle criteria, and derive a reference phase-velocity curve by phase-shift transform.
steps.quote: We call CC the cross-correlogram of the seismic traces of any possible receivers’ pair derived by a single shot.

steps.action: Take over the authors' earlier 2D common-midpoint CC grouping and modified FTAN frequency-velocity analysis.
steps.quote: under the 2D approach (Leontarakis et al., 2019), to group the CCs to specific positions (x, y) according to their midpoints

steps.action: Extend the analysis to 3D. CCs are grouped by midpoint and source-midpoint azimuth range. Frequency-velocity images are weighted toward a one-wavelength analysis to suppress cycle skipping, then stacked into azimuth-dependent 4D group and phase matrices. Velocities are picked semi-automatically within manually set fundamental-mode velocity ranges.
steps.quote: Then a weighted to one-wavelength, stacking-based procedure is followed to build an apparent dispersion image for each position (x,y)

steps.action: Build 'virtual' dispersion curves for every receiver pair from the azimuth-matched apparent velocity cube, using a wavelength-dependent quality factor, so that sources need not be aligned with receiver pairs.
steps.quote: We call these dispersion curves ‘virtual’, since they are not directly generated by the frequency analysis of real waveforms

steps.action: Adopt Eikonal tomography (Lin et al. 2009), with the smoothness-regularised penalty function of Jin & Gaherty (2015), to invert the virtual travel-times frequency by frequency into local dispersion curves.
steps.quote: Here, the Eikonal tomography method (Lin et al., 2009) is applied for the inversion of the virtual travel-times.

steps.action: Generate synthetic data: 12 m and 6 m checkerboard velocity models at 50 Hz, Eikonal forward travel-times for a dense layout with 2%, 4% and 6% Gaussian error, and sinusoids standing in for filtered CC waveforms.
steps.quote: the Eikonal equation is applied to calculate the surface wave propagation for each shot, using a fine discretization for the forward modelling

steps.action: Reconstruct the checkerboards with CMPCCST and with an in-line two-station tomography baseline, and score both against the true models by model RMS and correlation coefficient at each noise level.
steps.quote: the CMPCCST approach can greatly reconstruct both checkerboard models, for all Gaussian error data sets, thus proving the reliability of the proposed processing steps

steps.action: Design a real 3D test at a campus site with known conditions: borehole-based geotechnical model and a mapped cut-and-cover tunnel of known size and depth.
steps.quote: A real 3D seismic experiment was decided to be carried out at the campus of the National Technical University of Athens

steps.action: Use the 2009 geotechnical report, well logs and laboratory tests (three-layer 1D model) and the construction plans of the tunnel as reference.
steps.quote: a detailed geotechnical report and the respective well logs and laboratory measurements are still available

steps.action: Survey the site with 3D ERT (MOST technique) and FEM conductivity, which locate the tunnel and the resistivity layering.
steps.quote: The geophysical methods clearly depict the tunnel’s presence

steps.action: Acquire 3D active seismic data: 60 vertical 4.5 Hz geophones at about 3 m spacing over the tunnel, 68 weight-drop shots at 34 positions, RTK GPS coordinates.
steps.quote: An almost rectangular dense grid of 60 vertical 4.5 Hz geophones was deployed

steps.action: Apply CMPCCST to the test-site data: pre-processing, CC database, reference curve, scrubbing (coherency 0.2, offset 1 m, angle 60°, deviation 30°), rotated grid, six 30° azimuth ranges, and semi-automatic picking into apparent velocity cubes.
steps.quote: A scrubbing of the CCs that followed further analysis was undertaken, based on minimum CC coherency of 0.2

steps.action: Compare apparent velocities above and away from the tunnel across azimuths. The velocity difference peaks between N21 and N51, matching the tunnel direction.
steps.quote: This behaviour is indicative of the existence of a high-velocity contrast structure of semi-finite dimensions, such as the tunnel.

steps.action: Check the virtual dispersion curves of one receiver pair against dispersion images from three real near in-line CCs (stacked and individual). Also count usable pairs: 1770 virtual versus 502 or 1555 in-line pairs.
steps.quote: As shown, the virtual curves are well adapted to the local maxima that someone should manually pick in the dispersion images.

steps.action: Invert the virtual travel-times per frequency with a two-step residual-exclusion scheme to produce final azimuth-independent group and phase velocity cubes.
steps.quote: by following a two-step process in order to exclude measurement with travel-time residuals greater than an upper limit in seconds

steps.action: Compare the frequency band of the tunnel anomaly with the band expected from the wavelength/3 pseudo-depth rule (about 30 to over 60 Hz), and show the tunnel at 42 Hz.
steps.quote: the tunnel’s influence is expected to be revealed within a range from about 30 Hz to more than 60 Hz

steps.action: Jointly invert group and phase local dispersion curves (9-89 Hz) with a damped, smoothness-constrained 1D least-squares algorithm into a quasi-3D Vs model; the data misfit is below 5% RMS.
steps.quote: The quasi-3D Vs model, shown in Figure 18, was produced using the 1D joint inversion, mentioned earlier.

steps.action: Compare the Vs model with the borehole stratigraphy, the 3D ERT model and the tunnel position (a 600 m/s trace within 350 m/s at about 3 m depth).
steps.quote: The revealed layer sequence is well correlated with the stratigraphy corresponding to the geotechnical profile

steps.action: Explain the unexpectedly high Vs of the air-filled tunnel by the concrete shell acting as a high-Vs layer, while allowing higher-mode interference or mode conversion, and argue that these do not compromise the rest of the image.
steps.quote: Probably the concrete shell is providing a high Vs layer allowing Rayleigh waves to propagate at increased velocity.

steps.action: Acquire data at a noisy urban construction site in central Athens: 60 geophones on metal plates around an existing building, 37 shot positions, and a borehole-based 2D geotechnical section as reference.
steps.quote: An almost arbitrary dense grid of 60 vertical 4.5 Hz geophones was deployed

steps.action: Process with CMPCCST using two 90° azimuth ranges, chosen because weak lateral variation is expected. CC midpoints cover the area under the building. Joint 1D inversion gives a quasi-3D Vs model with misfit below 5% RMS.
steps.quote: since no severe or sharp lateral velocity variations are expected

steps.action: Compare the Vs section between boreholes G1 and G2 with the geotechnical cross-section, noting that resolution is lost with depth and at the edges.
steps.quote: The Vs cross-section, in general, is in good agreement with the 2D geotechnical cross-section, as proposed by the geotechnical experts

steps.action: Revise the geotechnical interpretation, placing the possible conglomerate bedrock at about 20 m rather than 15 m.
steps.quote: should not be considered until a depth of approximately 20 m in an updated geotechnical interpretation

steps.action: Keep the claim that CMPCCST maps frequency-dependent group and phase velocity and detects lateral and vertical Vs variations, with prerequisites on azimuthal source coverage, grid size and azimuthal partition.
steps.quote: The effectiveness of this alternative approach in detecting both lateral and in-depth shear-wave velocity variations was first confirmed by a controlled test site seismic experiment

tree.answer: Lateral and vertical near-surface Vs variations needing robust 3D mapping
No; inferred from surface-wave dispersion via tomography and inversion
Build and characterize a new processing method
No rival hypotheses; in-line two-station tomography used as baseline method
Set in synthetic checkerboards; found at a test site with known geology and tunnel
Survives noise levels 2-6%, two checkerboard sizes, real test site and a second noisy site

end.claim: CMP-CC stacking tomography automatically produces frequency-dependent group and phase velocity maps from active 3D networks and recovers lateral and in-depth Vs variations, as shown by checkerboard tests, a controlled test site and a noisy construction site.

decisive_move.sentence: The 3D azimuth-partitioned, one-wavelength-weighted CMP stacking that yields apparent velocity cubes, and from them virtual dispersion curves for all receiver pairs, is what the whole claim rests on.

gates.evidence: Action: the test site was chosen because its subsurface (boreholes, tunnel plans) was known, so the aim of testing the method directed acquisition, but no hypothesis about nature did (p. 50-51). Claim: the checkerboard reconstruction is scored against known models and could have failed (p. 50-51), but the field comparisons with geotechnical data are qualitative (p. 58, 61). Registration: the reference geotechnical models and tunnel geometry existed before the seismic data, and the expected 30-60 Hz tunnel band follows a stated rule (p. 57); processing parameters were not fixed in advance as far as the paper shows.

imports.item: spline interpolation (de Boor 1978) for the time-to-velocity transform
borehole logs, SPT and laboratory soil parameters used as reference models

novelty_claims.quote: Here, a new strategy that is well adapted to geotechnical investigations is proposed
It combines the advantages of a newly created commonmidpoint (CMP) cross-correlation (CC) analysis technique
Building reliable virtual dispersion curves for all the possible receiver pairs is an advantage of this method, compared to other straightray tomography approaches

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence was coded. The data are available only on request (p. 63). The synthetic tests ignore aliasing and higher-mode interference (p. 49) and use a single frequency. Uncertainty on the velocity cubes and Vs models is not quantified beyond data misfit (<5% RMS). The field validations against boreholes, ERT and the tunnel are visual and qualitative. Scrubbing thresholds, grid and azimuth partition were not varied on real data, so their effect is not reported. The high Vs of the air-filled tunnel was not predicted and is explained afterwards by the concrete shell or by higher modes (inference: a post hoc protective auxiliary). The 3D ERT and FEM surveys appear to predate this study ('have already been verified'), but the paper does not say when or by whom (inference). The capability_first composition fits only approximately: the walk is method construction followed by validation, with no later question about nature. Sub-claim: the revised bedrock depth of about 20 m at the construction site is a best_explanation-level interpretation, not independently confirmed.

disagreements.target: fully automated processing techniques commonly suggested for the SWT method
disagreements.support: The authors argue that higher modes dominate near-surface dispersion images and mislead automatic picking, and replace it with a semi-automatic picking scheme.
disagreements.quote: becomes difficult when using the fully automated processing techniques that are commonly [...]

disagreements.target: roll-along MASW approach (Foti; Park et al.)
disagreements.support: The point is argued from the literature; MASW gives 1D profiles and is slow to resolve sharp lateral variations, so the authors offer a 3D alternative.
disagreements.quote: it is somewhat difficult to accurately retrieve sharp lateral variations following a roll-along approach of MASW

disagreements.support: In checkerboard tests in-line tomography degrades at 6% noise (RMS 28.9-37.1%) while CMPCCST stays at 4.8-6.1%. Virtual curves give 1770 pairs versus 502 or 1555 in-line pairs.
disagreements.quote: [...] the necessity of alignment between the source and pair of receivers and reducing the number of shots

disagreements.target: 2D geotechnical cross-section by the geotechnical experts (construction site)
disagreements.support: The Vs model places the conglomerate bedrock at about 20 m rather than the 15 m assumed in the section, which the boreholes did not fully support.
disagreements.quote: should not be considered until a depth of approximately 20 m in an updated geotechnical interpretation

disagreements.target: geotechnical practice of analysing only phase velocity
disagreements.support: Group velocity proved more sensitive to Vs variations and correlated well with phase velocity, so the authors argue that joint inversion gives a more robust estimate.
disagreements.quote: Most geotechnical applications researchers pay attention only to the phase-velocity analysis

alternatives_considered.chosen: semi-automatic picking within manually defined velocity ranges
alternatives_considered.alternatives: manual picking of all dispersion images; fully automatic picking of velocity maxima
alternatives_considered.reason: manual picking is time-consuming; automatic picking can select higher modes in the near surface

alternatives_considered.chosen: virtual dispersion curves plus tomographic inversion of virtual travel-times
alternatives_considered.alternatives: omit the azimuth partition; average the azimuth-dependent apparent cubes
alternatives_considered.reason: each point of an averaged model would represent an area one wavelength in diameter

alternatives_considered.chosen: smoothness-constrained joint group and phase 1D least-squares inversion
alternatives_considered.alternatives: sparse / minimum-gradient-support inversions for sharp boundaries (Guillemoteau et al. 2022; Vignoli et al. 2021); individual group or phase inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: the aim is to evaluate the processing output, not the inversion algorithm
comparison of reliability and robustness to error

alternatives_considered.chosen: six 30° azimuth ranges (test site); two 90° ranges (construction site)
alternatives_considered.reason: depends on how severe the expected sharp lateral variations are; shorter ranges improve resolution but leave fewer CCs per group

alternatives_considered.chosen: virtual curves for all 1770 receiver pairs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: in-line pairs with CC-source deviation up to 1° (502 pairs) or 5° (1555 pairs)
alternatives_considered.reason: straight-ray coverage depends on source azimuthal coverage
